statement: Find all positive-integer sequences $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ such that, for each $n$, some positive integer $k$ satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_n/a_{n+i}=k$.
ratingReason: The least term anchors an equality case; the resulting constant tail must then be propagated backwards.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
The constant positive-integer sequences work. Conversely, let $m$ be the least value occurring and choose $a_N=m$. Every summand $m/a_{N+i}$ is at most $1$. Their sum equals their number, so each is $1$, in particular $a_{N+1}=m$. Repeating at $N+1,N+2,\ldots$ shows that the whole tail equals $m$.

Now apply the equation at $N-1$. All its denominators equal $m$, giving $k a_{N-1}/m=k$, hence $a_{N-1}=m$. Continue backwards to obtain $a_n=m$ for every $n$.

statement: In an unknown finite connected graph, two vertices $A,B$ are distinguished. You know only the multiset of values $\max(d(v,A),d(v,B))$ over all vertices $v$, where distance counts edges. Find the smallest universal $N$ allowing $d(A,B)$ to be narrowed to at most $N$ possibilities.
ratingReason: A shortest-path midpoint gives a sharp two-value bound. Showing two are sometimes necessary requires two graphs with exactly the same observed multiset.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Let $\mu$ be the smallest listed value and put $d=d(A,B)$. The triangle inequality gives $d\le d(v,A)+d(v,B)\le2\max(d(v,A),d(v,B))$, so $d\le2\mu$.

A middle vertex of a shortest $A$–$B$ path has maximum distance $\lceil d/2\rceil$. Thus $\mu=\lceil d/2\rceil$ and $d\in\{2\mu-1,2\mu\}$. Two possibilities always suffice.

On a cycle of length four, choose adjacent vertices as $A,B$, or choose opposite vertices. In both cases the observed multiset is $\{1,1,2,2\}$, while the distances are respectively $1$ and $2$. Therefore $\boxed{N=2}$ is best possible.

statement: Find all $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that $f^5(x+y)=f^2(x)+y+1$ for all real $x,y$, where superscripts denote iteration.

solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Set $y=-x$. There is a constant $c$ such that $f^2(x)=x+c$ for every $x$. Therefore $f^4(x)=x+2c$ and $f^5(x)=f(x+2c)$.

The equation with $y=0$ gives $f(x+2c)=x+c+1$. Replacing $x+2c$ by $t$ yields $f(t)=t+1-c$. Its second iterate is then $t+2-2c$, which must equal $t+c$. Hence $c=2/3$ and $\boxed{f(t)=t+1/3}$.

Direct substitution verifies the answer.

statement: Let $0<x_1<\cdots<x_{2024}=1$. Colour half the numbers red and half blue, listing each colour increasingly as $r_i,b_i$; put $b_0=0$ and $S=\sum_{i=1}^{1012}r_i(b_i-b_{i-1})$. solutionCredit: Original English exposition; official Danish solution also linked
solution:
Write $n=1012$. For any colouring, positivity gives
$$S=\sum_{i=1}^n r_i(b_i-b_{i-1})\le r_nb_n\le x_{2023}.$$
For (a), choose $x_i=i/4048$ for $1\le i\le2023$ and $x_{2024}=1$.
Then every colouring has $S<1/2$.

For (b), colour the two largest entries differently and distribute the others
so that each colour occurs $n$ times. Then $r_nb_n=x_{2023}$. Set $r_0=0$.
The colouring obtained by exchanging red and blue has sum
$$T=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i(r_i-r_{i-1}).$$
Put $\Delta r_i=r_i-r_{i-1}$ and $\Delta b_i=b_i-b_{i-1}$. The identity
$$r_i\Delta b_i+b_i\Delta r_i
=r_ib_i-r_{i-1}b_{i-1}+\Delta r_i\Delta b_i$$
telescopes to
$$S+T=r_nb_n+\sum_{i=1}^n\Delta r_i\Delta b_i>x_{2023}.$$
Every increment is positive. Hence at least one of these two colourings has
sum greater than $x_{2023}/2$, as required.

statement:
A square $ABCD$ has its bottom vertex $A$ on a horizontal line, with $B$ to the left and $D$ to the right above that line. Place two upright squares on the line: $B$ is the upper-right corner of the left square, and $D$ the upper-left corner of the right one. Let $E,F$ be their other upper corners.

Construct squares on $EC$ and $CF$, on the sides of those lines opposite $A$. Let $U,V$ be their respective new vertices adjacent to $C$. Prove that triangle $UCV$ and square $ABCD$ have equal areas.

![Five squares surrounding the target triangle](assets/diagrams/denmark-2026-q4.svg)
ratingReason: The five-square picture must be converted into compatible lengths or rotated vectors. A determinant or an auxiliary-rectangle decomposition then reveals the area identity.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Choose coordinates $A=(0,0)$, $B=(-b,a)$ and $D=(a,b)$, with $a,b>0$. Then $C=(a-b,a+b)$ and the central square has area $a^2+b^2$.

The two upright squares give $E=(-a-b,a)$ and $F=(a+b,b)$, so $\overrightarrow{EC}=(2a,b)$ and $\overrightarrow{CF}=(2b,-a)$. Rotating the relevant side vectors through a right angle in the outward direction gives
$$\overrightarrow{CU}=(-b,2a),\qquad \overrightarrow{CV}=(a,2b).$$
Consequently the area of $UCV$ is
$$\frac12\left|(-b)(2b)-(2a)a\right|=a^2+b^2,$$
exactly the area of the central square.

statement: Find all positive integer solutions of $(x+y)^2=100x+y$.
ratingReason: Introducing the sum bounds the search and forces a consecutive-product congruence modulo99; coprimality reduces this to four residue classes.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Set $s=x+y$. Then $s(s-1)=99x$. Since $0<x<s$, we have $1<s\le99$. Also $99\mid s(s-1)$.

Consecutive integers are coprime. Hence each of $9$ and $11$ divides either $s$ or $s-1$, so modulo $99$ we have $s\equiv0,1,45,55$. In the interval $1<s\le99$, this leaves $s=45,55,99$.

Recovering $x=s(s-1)/99$ and $y=s-x$ gives exactly $\boxed{(20,25),(30,25),(98,1)}$. Direct substitution verifies all three.

statement: Three perfect logicians A, B and C each have a positive integer on their forehead. Each sees the other two numbers, knows that one number is the sum of the other two, and knows that everyone reasons perfectly. Asked in order, A, B and C each say they cannot determine their own number. Asked again, A correctly announces $65$. Find all three numbers.
ratingReason: Each announcement eliminates entire proportional families. A complete fourth-round classification is needed; noticing one plausible triple does not establish uniqueness.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Write a triple in the order $(A,B,C)$. A person seeing $u,v$ considers $u+v$ and $|u-v|$, with zero forbidden. In the following lists, every triple may be multiplied by any positive integer.

A would know immediately exactly for $(2,1,1)$, so the first answer excludes that family.

At B's turn, the newly excluded families are $(1,2,1)$ (equal visible numbers) and $(2,3,1)$ (B's other candidate gives the already excluded $(2,1,1)$).

At C's turn, the newly excluded families are
$$ (1,1,2),\quad(2,1,3),\quad(1,2,3),\quad(2,3,5). $$
The first has equal visible numbers. In each other case, changing C's number to the other candidate gives one of the earlier excluded families. These lists are exhaustive: the only reasons to know are equal visible numbers or an alternative already ruled out.

For A to know on the fourth turn, changing A's value must produce one of those six previously excluded families, while the actual triple must have survived all three answers. The possibilities are exactly
$$ (3,2,1),\ (4,3,1),\ (3,1,2),\ (4,1,3),\ (5,2,3),\ (8,3,5). $$
All are primitive integer triples, so their scale factors must be integers. Only $5$ among their first coordinates divides $65$. Thus $\boxed{(A,B,C)=(65,26,39)}$.

This triple does survive the first three answers; A's alternative $13$ would give $(13,26,39)$, a multiple of $(1,2,3)$, in which C would have known. Hence A's final announcement is justified.
notes: English mathematical paraphrase of the official paper. Year denotes the actual sitting year. The English statement renames the three participants. The original solution omits some elimination cases; the complete classification is supplied here.

Ignore the fixed entry $3$. The other entries form three cycles, with lengths $4,2,2$: $(1,8,6,5)$, $(2,7)$ and $(4,9)$.

A cycle of length $r$ can be repaired in $r+1$ moves: move one of its entries into the spare box, fill the newly empty position with its correct entry, continue around the cycle, then return the parked entry to its correct position. This gives $5+3+3=11$ moves.

For the lower bound, each of the eight initially misplaced entries must eventually be moved into its final position. For each original cycle, consider the first move involving one of its entries. No box of that cycle is empty before this move, so the entry moves outside the cycle and is not placed correctly. This is an additional move, distinct for each of the three cycles. Thus at least $8+3=\boxed{11}$ moves are necessary.

statement: Assign a colour to each nonempty subset of an $n$-element set, where $n\ge1$. Two subsets with a common element must receive different colours. What is the minimum number of colours?

solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Fix an element $a$. There are $2^{n-1}$ subsets containing $a$, and all must have different colours. Thus at least $2^{n-1}$ colours are needed.

Pair each subset $S$ with its complement. The $2^n$ subsets form $2^{n-1}$ pairs, and the members of a pair are disjoint. Assign a different colour to each pair, omitting the empty subset. This is valid and uses exactly $\boxed{2^{n-1}}$ colours.

statement: Let $m\ge3$ be an integer. Count the integers $x$ with $0<x<m(m-1)$ for which $m\mid x-1$ and $m(m-1)\mid x(x-1)$. Give the answer for $m=2025$ and in general.
ratingReason: A substitution reduces the condition to consecutive factors modulo m−1; independence of prime-power choices and the endpoint range must both be justified.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Write $x=km+1$. The given range is equivalent to $0\le k\le m-2$, so $k$ traverses every residue class modulo $m-1$ exactly once. Cancelling $m$ in the second divisibility condition gives
$$m-1\mid k(km+1),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad m-1\mid k(k+1).$$
Factor $m-1=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$. Since consecutive integers are coprime, each prime power must divide exactly one of $k,k+1$. Thus $k\equiv0$ or $-1\pmod{p_i^{e_i}}$, independently for every $i$.

The Chinese remainder theorem gives exactly $\boxed{2^r}$ allowed values. For $2025$, we have $2024=2^3\cdot11\cdot23$, giving $\boxed8$.

statement: For a fixed positive integer $k$, classify all functions $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ satisfying $f(f(n))=n+k$ for every positive integer $n$.
ratingReason: Commuting the function with its second iterate reveals periodic translation. Complete classification then requires pairing residue classes and controlling which class receives the extra shift.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
There are no solutions for odd $k$. For even $k$, all solutions are obtained as follows. Partition $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ into unordered pairs, choose an ordering $(a,b)$ for each pair, and define, for $q\ge0$,
$$f(a+qk)=b+qk,\qquad f(b+qk)=a+(q+1)k.$$
These formulas clearly give $f^2(n)=n+k$.

For completeness, evaluating $f^3(n)$ in two ways yields $f(n+k)=f(n)+k$. Thus the first $k$ values determine $f$. Their residues modulo $k$ cover all classes, because $f^2$ does; hence they define a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,\ldots,k\}$.

Write $f(i)=\pi(i)+q_i k$, with $q_i\ge0$. Then
$$f^2(i)=\pi^2(i)+(q_i+q_{\pi(i)})k=i+k.$$
Comparison of residues and quotients gives $\pi^2(i)=i$ and $q_i+q_{\pi(i)}=1$. A fixed point is impossible, since it would require $2q_i=1$. Consequently $\pi$ pairs the residue classes, and on each pair the two shifts are $0$ and $1$. This proves the claimed classification and forces $k$ to be even.

statement: Prove that for every pair of positive integers $k,n$, there exist integers $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ such that $n=x_1+x_2^2+\cdots+x_k^k$ and $0\le x_j\le2^{k-1}n^{1/k}$ for every $j$.
ratingReason: Greedily removing a kth power is natural, but the remainder estimate must be strong enough for the induction to preserve a uniform kth-root bound.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
We also allow $n=0$, when all entries can be zero. Induct on $k$; $k=1$ is immediate.

For $k\ge2$, put $t=n^{1/k}$, $x_k=\lfloor t\rfloor$, and $r=n-x_k^k$. Factoring the power difference gives
$$0\le r=(t-x_k)\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t^{k-1-i}x_k^i\le k t^{k-1}\le2^{k-1}t^{k-1}.$$
The induction hypothesis represents $r$ as $x_1+\cdots+x_{k-1}^{k-1}$ with
$$x_j\le2^{k-2}r^{1/(k-1)}\le2^{k-1}t.$$
Also $x_k\le t$. Together these give the requested representation and bounds.

statement: On an $n\times n$ board, a player wants to place exactly one cross and one circle in every row and column, with at most one symbol per cell. Beforehand, an opponent may forbid a cross or forbid a circle in selected cells, with at most one prohibition per cell. Minimise the larger of the two prohibition counts needed to make the placement impossible.
ratingReason: A collision construction gives an upper bound, while cyclic diagonals simultaneously provide many disjoint permutation placements for the lower bound.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
The answer is $\boxed{n-1}$; for $n=1$ the requested placement is already impossible with no prohibitions.

For $n\ge2$, forbid crosses in $(1,2),\ldots,(1,n)$ and circles in $(2,1),\ldots,(n,1)$. A cross in the first row and a circle in the first column would both be forced into $(1,1)$. Thus $n-1$ prohibitions of each type suffice.

Conversely, partition the board into the $n$ cyclic diagonals $j-i\equiv r\pmod n$. Each diagonal contains one cell in every row and column. If there are at most $n-2$ cross prohibitions, at least two diagonals are entirely available for crosses. Likewise at least two are available for circles. Choose one of the former and a different one of the latter. The two diagonals are disjoint and give a valid placement. Hence fewer than $n-1$ of each type cannot block the player.

statement: An orange, banana and lemon each have a positive integer price. Four oranges, three bananas and a lemon cost the same as three oranges and two lemons. A friend knows the total price $M$ of three oranges and two lemons, but cannot determine the three prices. For every smaller attainable total, the prices would be uniquely determined. Find $M$.
ratingReason: The logical statement must be converted into the first repeated value of a two-variable positive-integer linear form, then an extremal pair of representations identified.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Let the prices be $a,b,c$. The equality gives $c=a+3b$, hence $M=3a+2c=5a+6b$.

Two distinct positive representations satisfy $5(a-a')=6(b'-b)$. Their $a$-values differ by at least $6$ and their $b$-values by at least $5$. In the representation with the smaller $a$, we therefore have $a\ge1,b\ge6$, giving $M\ge5+36=41$.

At $M=41$, the representations $(a,b)=(1,6)$ and $(7,1)$ both work, with $c=19$ and $10$. Thus the first ambiguous attainable total is $\boxed{41}$.

statement: Four labelled coins initially occupy the vertices of a square. A move reflects one coin in the position of another coin, which stays fixed. Can a finite sequence of moves leave the coins at the vertices of a square with a different side length?
ratingReason: A lattice invariant rules out shrinking; reversibility and similarity must then be combined to rule out enlargement as well.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Scale and rotate so the original square has vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$. A move replaces a point $X$ by $2Y-X$, so every coin retains integer coordinates. Distinct lattice points are at least distance $1$ apart; therefore a smaller square is impossible.

Every move is its own inverse. If a sequence reached a square of side $s>1$, its reverse would take that labelled square back to a unit square. Apply a similarity of ratio $1/s$ carrying the larger square to a unit square. Reflections in coin positions commute with similarities, so the same reverse instructions would take a unit square to one of side $1/s<1$, contradicting the lattice argument. Hence the side length cannot change.

statement: (a) Give a function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that $0<f(x)<f(x+f(x))<\sqrt2x$ for all $x>0$. (b) Prove that no function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $x<f(x+f(x))<\sqrt2f(x)$ for all $x>0$.
ratingReason: The existence example is easy, but impossibility requires repeatedly improving a global lower bound and feeding it back into the shifted argument.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
(a) The function $f(x)=x/2$ works, since $f(x+f(x))=3x/4$.

(b) Suppose such a function exists. The given chain first implies $f(x)>x/\sqrt2>0$. Applying this bound at $x+f(x)>0$ gives
$$\sqrt2f(x)>f(x+f(x))>\frac{x+f(x)}{\sqrt2},$$
so $f(x)>x$. Applying the improved bound at the same argument now yields $\sqrt2f(x)>x+f(x)$, hence $f(x)>(1+\sqrt2)x$.

One last substitution gives
$$\sqrt2f(x)>f(x+f(x))>(1+\sqrt2)(x+f(x))>\sqrt2f(x),$$
a contradiction.

statement: Find the largest positive integer which cannot be written $a+bc$ with positive integers $a<b<c$.
ratingReason: One must prove eventual representability, not just search small values. A division-with-remainder interpretation leads to a least-common-multiple bound or a careful construction near consecutive squares.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
The answer is $\boxed{24}$. Indeed, if $24=a+bc$ with $0<a<b<c$, then $b\in\{2,3,4\}$. Each such $b$ divides $24$, whereas division by $b$ would have nonzero remainder $a$, impossible.

For $25\le n\le29$, use respectively
$$25=1+4\cdot6,\quad26=2+3\cdot8,\quad27=1+2\cdot13,\quad28=1+3\cdot9,\quad29=1+2\cdot14.$$
Now let $n\ge30$, and choose $k\ge5$ with $k(k+1)\le n<(k+1)(k+2)$. If any $2\le b\le k$ fails to divide $n$, division gives $n=bc+a$ with $0<a<b$ and $c\ge b+1$, a valid representation.

Otherwise $n$ is divisible by every integer up to $k$. For $k=5$, this forces $n\ge60$, contradicting $n<42$. For $k\ge6$,
$$n\ge\operatorname{lcm}(k-2,k-1,k)\ge\frac{k(k-1)(k-2)}2>(k+1)(k+2).$$
For the last inequality, writing $k=6+t$ reduces twice the difference to $t^3+13t^2+44t+8>0$. This again contradicts the choice of $k$. Therefore every $n>24$ is representable.

statement: How many integers $1\le n\le2020$ satisfy $2020\mid n(n+1)(n+2)$?
ratingReason: The factors4,5 and101 impose independent residue restrictions; the square factor4 needs separate attention before the Chinese remainder theorem can be applied.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Since $2020=4\cdot5\cdot101$, all three factors must divide the product. Modulo each of $4,5,101$, the admissible residues of $n$ are exactly $0,-1,-2$. For modulus $4$, the only other residue $1$ gives product $1\cdot2\cdot3\equiv2$, so it fails.

The moduli are pairwise coprime. Each of the $3^3$ combinations gives exactly one residue modulo $2020$, and the interval $1,\ldots,2020$ contains each residue once. The answer is $\boxed{27}$.

statement: Classify all bounded functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(f(x)+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for every real $x,y$.
ratingReason: The equation makes the range closed under addition. Iterating one nonzero output contradicts boundedness; no regularity assumption such as continuity is needed.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
If $u=f(a)$ is any value in the range, define $x_1=a$ and $x_{j+1}=f(x_j)+a$. The equation gives $f(x_{j+1})=f(x_j)+u$, so by induction $f(x_j)=ju$.

If $u\ne0$, this contradicts boundedness. Thus every output is zero. Conversely $\boxed{f\equiv0}$ satisfies the equation.

statement: Find the least $n$ for which a simple, nondegenerate polygon with integer-coordinate vertices can have side lengths $1,2,\ldots,n$, in some order.
ratingReason: Parity eliminates two sizes, while the remaining small cases require geometric restrictions. A valid non-self-intersecting lattice construction is also essential.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
The answer is $\boxed7$. Three sides of lengths $1,2,3$ give a degenerate triangle. A lattice segment of integer length at most $4$ must be horizontal or vertical; hence a nondegenerate four-sided polygon with those lengths would have to be a rectangle, impossible with four distinct lengths.

For any lattice segment with integer length $d$ and coordinate differences $u,v$, we have $u+v\equiv u^2+v^2=d^2\equiv d\pmod2$. Summing around a closed polygon shows its integer perimeter is even. For $n=5,6$, the perimeter is respectively $15,21$, excluding both.

For $n=7$, take the successive vertices
$$(0,0),(1,0),(1,-2),(4,-2),(4,2),(-3,2),(-3,-4).$$
Their side lengths are $1,2,3,4,7,6,5$. The six axis-parallel segments and final diagonal meet only at neighbouring endpoints, giving the required simple polygon.

statement: Find all integers $a$ for which some prime $p\ge5$ divides $\displaystyle\sum_{j=2}^{p-3}\binom{p-1}{j}a^{j-2}$.
ratingReason: Binomial coefficients modulo a prime reveal a truncated geometric sum. The remaining existence question requires classifying when a quadratic has only the prime factor3.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Write the sum as $X_p(a)$. Modulo $p$, $\binom{p-1}{j}\equiv(-1)^j$. Thus
$$X_p(a)\equiv\sum_{r=0}^{p-5}(-a)^r.$$
If $a\equiv0$, the sum is $1$; if $a\equiv-1$, it is $p-4\not\equiv0$. Otherwise geometric summation and Fermat's theorem give
$$a^3X_p(a)\equiv a^2-a+1.$$
Therefore the desired prime exists exactly when $a^2-a+1$ has a prime divisor at least $5$; such a divisor automatically avoids $a=0,-1$ modulo $p$.

The quadratic is positive and odd. If it has no such prime divisor, it is a power of $3$. When $3$ divides it, $a=3t-1$, and
$$a^2-a+1=3(3t^2-3t+1),$$
so its exponent of $3$ is exactly one. Hence the only excluded cases satisfy $a^2-a+1=1$ or $3$, giving $a=0,1,-1,2$.

The answer is all integers except $\boxed{-1,0,1,2}$.

statement: A finite collection of closed cubes in three-dimensional space has all edges parallel to the coordinate axes. No point belongs to more than $M$ cubes. Prove that the cubes can be partitioned into at most $8(M-1)+1$ groups, each consisting of pairwise disjoint cubes.

solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Choose a cube $Q$ of least side length. Any other cube meeting it has at least that side length. In each coordinate, an interval of at least the length of $Q$'s interval that intersects it must contain an endpoint of it. Consequently every cube meeting $Q$ contains at least one of $Q$'s eight vertices.

At each vertex, at most $M-1$ other cubes can occur. Hence $Q$ meets at most $8(M-1)$ other cubes.

Induct on the collection size. Colour all cubes other than $Q$ with $8(M-1)+1$ colours so that intersecting cubes have different colours. At most $8(M-1)$ colours are used on neighbours of $Q$, leaving an available colour for it. Colour classes are the required groups.

statement: Let $\Omega$ be the closed unit disk. Find the least real $r$ for which three points can be chosen in $\Omega$ so that every closed disk contained in $\Omega$ with radius greater than $r$ contains at least one chosen point.
ratingReason: A sharp result needs both an empty-sector obstruction for every placement and a carefully scaled equilateral placement whose interception property must be proved.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Put $\rho=\sqrt3/(2+\sqrt3)$ and $\gamma=(1-\rho)/2$, so $\rho=\sqrt3\gamma$.

For a lower bound, divide the unit disk into three $120^\circ$ sectors, choosing a sector boundary through one of the three proposed points. At least one sector has no proposed point in its interior. The largest disk inscribed in that sector has radius $\rho$: if its centre is distance $d$ from the unit-disk centre, then its radius is $d\sin60^\circ$ and also $1-d$. For any $r<\rho$, shrink that disk slightly to a radius still greater than $r$. It lies strictly inside the sector and misses all three points. Thus $r\ge\rho$.

For the matching construction, choose three equally spaced points on the concentric circle of radius $\gamma$. Consider any disk of radius $R>\rho$ contained in $\Omega$, with centre distance $d\le1-R$ from the origin. If it contains the entire small circle, we are done. Otherwise its intersection with that circle is an arc. The half-angle $\theta$ of that arc satisfies
$$\cos\theta=\frac{d^2+\gamma^2-R^2}{2\gamma d}.$$
Here $d>0$ and $R>\gamma$. For fixed $R$, the expression increases with $d$, so it is at most its value at $d=1-R$. Writing $t=1-R<2\gamma$, that value is
$$\frac{2t+\gamma^2-1}{2\gamma t},$$
which increases with $t$. At $t=2\gamma$ it equals $1/2$, using $\rho^2=3\gamma^2$. Hence $\theta>60^\circ$. The arc has length greater than $120^\circ$ in angle and contains one of the three equally spaced points.

Therefore the least value is $\boxed{r=\sqrt3/(2+\sqrt3)}$.

statement: A strictly increasing function $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ satisfies $f(f(n))=3n$ for every $n$. Determine $f(2019)$.
ratingReason: Iterating at powers of3 gives anchor values. Strict increase then fills entire integer intervals exactly, after which the second iterate controls the alternating intervals.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
First $f(1)=2$: the value $1$ contradicts $f^2(1)=3$, while $f(1)\ge3$ would force $f(f(1))\ge f(3)\ge5$. Hence $f(2)=3$.

Evaluating $f^3(n)$ in two ways gives $f(3n)=3f(n)$. Thus for $a=3^k$,
$$f(a)=2a,\qquad f(2a)=3a.$$
There are exactly $a-1$ integers between each pair of endpoints. Strict increase therefore forces $f(a+j)=2a+j$ for $0\le j\le a$.

Applying $f$ again yields
$$f(2a+j)=3(a+j)\qquad(0\le j\le a).$$
Since $2019=2\cdot729+561$, take $a=729=3^6$ to obtain $\boxed{f(2019)=3(729+561)=3870}$.

statement: Does there exist a sequence containing each positive integer exactly once such that every sum of consecutive terms is a perfect square?
ratingReason: A greedy square-sum choice need not visit every integer. A controlled three-term bridge must reach the least omitted integer while keeping all added terms fresh.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Yes. Build finite initial segments, always preserving distinctness and the square-sum condition. Start with $1$. Suppose the current last term is $L$, and let $c$ be the least positive integer not yet used.

Choose an arbitrarily large integer $N$ of such parity that $a=N^2-L$ has parity opposite to $c$. Put
$$x=\frac{a-c-1}{2},\qquad b=x^2-c.$$
By choosing $N$ sufficiently large, we ensure that $a$ exceeds every previously used term and $b>a$. This is possible because $b$ grows quadratically in $a$.

Append $a,b,c$. They are positive, distinct and unused, and
$$L+a=N^2,\qquad a+b=(x+1)^2,\qquad b+c=x^2.$$
Thus the construction can continue. Each stage includes the least omitted positive integer, so every positive integer eventually appears, exactly once.

For attainment use

Start at $0$ and follow the desired comparisons greedily. After any selected term, among the next two entries there is one larger and one smaller than it. Thus each comparison requires advancing at most two positions. After $m$ comparisons the chosen subsequence ends by position $2m+1$, proving that every pattern occurs.

statement: Two internal rays trisect angle $A$ of triangle $ABC$, meeting $BC$ at $P,Q$ in that order. Find the least constant $K$ such that $PQ\le K(BP+QC)$ for every triangle. Determine whether equality is possible.
ratingReason: Two angle-bisector length identities yield a strict product bound; AM–GM gives the inequality, and a degenerating family is needed to prove the constant optimal.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Write $AB=c$, $AC=b$, $AP=s$, $AQ=t$, and $BP=x$, $PQ=y$, $QC=z$. In triangle $ABQ$, the ray $AP$ is an angle bisector, giving $s^2=ct-xy<ct$. Similarly $t^2=bs-yz<bs$. Multiplying yields $st<bc$.

The angle-bisector theorem also gives $x/y=c/t$ and $z/y=b/s$. Hence
$$x+z=y\left(\frac ct+\frac bs\right)\ge2y\sqrt{\frac{bc}{st}}>2y.$$
Thus $K=1/2$ works and equality is never attained.

To see optimality, take isosceles triangles with fixed altitude from $A$ and let the base tend to zero. Then $b=c$, $s=t$, and all four lengths tend to that altitude. Therefore $(x+z)/y=c/t+b/s$ tends to $2$. No smaller $K$ works, so $\boxed{K=1/2}$.

solution:
It is reducible exactly when $n$ is not a power of $3$.

If $n=3^k m$ with $m>1$ and $3\nmid m$, then $1+t^m+t^{2m}$ is divisible in $\mathbb Z[t]$ by $1+t+t^2$: modulo the latter polynomial, $t^3=1$, and the exponents $0,m,2m$ represent all three residue classes modulo $3$. Substitute $t=x^{3^k}$ to obtain a nontrivial factorisation.

Conversely let $n=3^k$. Over $\mathbb F_3$ the polynomial becomes
$$1+x^n+x^{2n}=(x^2+x+1)^{3^k}=(x-1)^{2n}.$$
If it factored as nonconstant integer polynomials, we could take both factors monic. Their reductions modulo $3$ retain their positive degrees, so each is a positive power of $x-1$. Both factors therefore have values at $x=1$ divisible by $3$. Their product at $1$ would be divisible by $9$, whereas the given polynomial has value $3$. Contradiction.

statement: For a prime $p$, determine all coprime positive integers $m,n$ satisfying $\dfrac{p+m}{p+n}=\dfrac mn+\dfrac1{p^2}$.
ratingReason: Clearing denominators first forces a prime divisor of n; coprimality then makes the remaining multiplier divide p, reducing the equation to two carefully separated cases.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Clearing denominators gives $(n-m)p^3=n(p+n)$, so $p\mid n$. Write $n=kp$; division by $p^2$ yields
$$pm=k(p^2-k-1).$$
Because $\gcd(m,n)=1$, also $\gcd(m,k)=1$, so $k\mid p$. Thus $k=1$ or $k=p$.

If $k=1$, then $pm=p^2-2$, forcing $p=2$ and $(m,n)=(1,2)$. If $k=p$, then $m=p^2-p-1$ and $n=p^2$; these are positive and coprime for every prime $p$.

Direct substitution verifies the answers: $\boxed{(p^2-p-1,p^2)}$ always, with the extra pair $\boxed{(1,2)}$ only when $p=2$.

statement: Find the smallest constant $C$ such that $S\le C(ab+bc+ca)$ for every triangle with side lengths $a,b,c$ and area $S$.
ratingReason: The sharp equilateral value needs a proof for all triangles; a semiperimeter substitution turns Heron’s formula into two linked symmetric inequalities.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Set $a=x+y$, $b=y+z$, $c=z+x$ with $x,y,z>0$. Write $p=x+y+z$, $q=xy+yz+zx$, $r=xyz$. Then
$$ab+bc+ca=p^2+q,\qquad S^2=pr.$$
The elementary inequalities $p^2\ge3q$ and $q^2\ge3pr$ give
$$ (ab+bc+ca)^2=(p^2+q)^2\ge16q^2\ge48pr=48S^2.$$
Both equalities hold when $x=y=z$, i.e. for an equilateral triangle. Thus the optimal constant is $\boxed{C=1/(4\sqrt3)=\sqrt3/12}$.

statement: Real numbers $a,b,c,x,y,z$ satisfy $x+y+z=0$, $a+b+c\ge0$ and $ab+bc+ca\ge0$. Prove $ax^2+by^2+cz^2\ge0$.

solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
If $a+b+c=0$, then $a^2+b^2+c^2=(a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca)\le0$, so $a=b=c=0$ and the claim is immediate.

Otherwise $a+b+c>0$, so at least one pair sum is positive. Relabel the corresponding coefficients and variables so that $a+b>0$. Since $z=-x-y$, direct expansion gives
$$ (a+b)(ax^2+by^2+cz^2)=(ax-by)^2+(ab+bc+ca)(x+y)^2\ge0.$$
Division by $a+b$ proves the result.

statement: Two existing fence segments of length $20$ meet at a right angle. Let $A$ be the free end of one segment. Can two further straight fence segments, of lengths $13$ and $14$, be joined to form a path from $A$ to a point on the other existing segment, enclosing an area of at least $200$?
ratingReason: One must choose a non-obvious closing point so that the added triangle is feasible and sufficiently large; Heron’s formula verifies an exact construction.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Yes. Let the corner be $O$, with $OA=20$, and choose $B$ on the other segment with $OB=15$. Then $AB=25$.

Construct triangle $APB$ on the side of $AB$ opposite $O$, with $AP=13$ and $PB=14$. It exists because $13+14>25$. Its semiperimeter is $26$, so its area is
$$\sqrt{26(26-13)(26-14)(26-25)}=26\sqrt6.$$
The enclosed quadrilateral $OAPB$ has area $150+26\sqrt6>200$, since $(26\sqrt6)^2=4056>2500$. This is a valid placement within the angle between the existing fence rays.

statement: A convex cyclic trapezoid $ABCD$ has $AB\parallel CD$. Its circumcircle has radius $R$ and centre on $AB$. A point $E$ on the circle satisfies $\angle DAE=90^\circ$ and $AE/AB=3/4$. Determine all four side lengths of the trapezoid.
ratingReason: Recognising both diameters and the isosceles trapezoid reduces the problem to two right-triangle relations; the shorter base then requires recovering a chord’s projection.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Since the circle centre lies on $AB$, we have $AB=2R$ and $AE=3R/2$. The right angle $DAE$ makes $DE$ another diameter, so
$$AD^2=(2R)^2-(3R/2)^2=7R^2/4.$$
A cyclic trapezoid is isosceles, hence $BC=AD=R\sqrt7/2$.

Place $A=(-R,0)$, $B=(R,0)$ and $D=(u,v)$ on the circle. Then
$$AD^2=(u+R)^2+v^2=2R^2+2Ru=7R^2/4,$$
giving $u=-R/8$. Symmetry puts $C=(R/8,v)$, so $CD=R/4$.

Thus $\boxed{AB=2R,\ CD=R/4,\ AD=BC=R\sqrt7/2}$.

statement: Find all primes $p$ such that $p+1$ equals the product of all primes smaller than $p$.
ratingReason: Prime factors of nearby smaller odd numbers are forced to divide tiny differences. Two such restrictions then contradict a simple modulus.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
Checking $p=2,3,5,7$ leaves only $p=5$, which works.

Suppose $p\ge11$ works. Every prime divisor of $p-2$ is smaller than $p$, so it divides the product $p+1$. Hence it divides $3$, and $p-2=3^u$ for some $u\ge1$.

Similarly every prime divisor of $p-6$ divides both $p-6$ and $p+1$, hence is $7$. Therefore $p-6=7^v$ for some $v\ge1$.

Subtracting gives $3^u=7^v+4$, impossible modulo $3$ since its right side is $2$ modulo $3$. Thus $\boxed{p=5}$ is the only solution.

statement: Each cell of a $13\times13$ board is black or white. A move reverses all colours in a contiguous $2\times2$ or $9\times9$ subsquare. Is it always possible to make the whole board black?
ratingReason: The useful invariant is restricted to two central rows, chosen so every large move covers both and every small move changes an even number of their cells.
solutionCredit: Independent mathematical exposition for Olympiad Atlas
solution:
No. Number rows $1,\ldots,13$, and consider the parity of the number of white cells in rows $6$ and $7$ together.

A $2\times2$ move meets these rows in $0,2$ or $4$ cells. Every $9\times9$ subsquare contains both central rows, so it meets them in $18$ cells. Thus every move changes an even number of cells in the chosen set and preserves the parity of its white count.

Start with exactly one white cell in row $7$, all other cells black. The invariant is odd, while an all-black board has even count zero. Therefore this colouring cannot reach all black.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, a diameter of its circumcircle passes through the midpoint of $BC$ and meets $AC$ at $D$. Prove that $AD:DC=1:3$ if and only if $\tan B=2\tan C$.
ratingReason: The diameter supplies an isosceles triangle; a sine-rule ratio then translates the length condition into a tangent identity.
solution:
The diameter through the midpoint of chord $BC$ lies on its perpendicular bisector, so $DB=DC$. Hence $\angle DBC=C$ and $\angle ABD=B-C$. By the sine rule in $ABD$,
$$\frac{AD}{DC}=\frac{\sin(B-C)}{\sin A}=\frac{\sin(B-C)}{\sin(B+C)}.$$
The ratio is $1/3$ precisely when $\sin(B+C)=3\sin(B-C)$. Expanding gives $\sin B\cos C=2\cos B\sin C$. Since $B,C$ are acute, division by $\cos B\cos C$ gives the stated equivalence.

statement: Determine all integer pairs $(x,y)$ for which $x^3+y^3=-2015$.
ratingReason: Factorization reduces the problem to divisors of 2015, but a size bound and cubic residues sharply reduce the cases before solving the remaining quadratic.
solution:
Write $s=-(x+y)>0$. Factoring gives $s(x^2-xy+y^2)=2015$. Since $x^2-xy+y^2\ge(x+y)^2/4$, we have $s^3\le8060$. As $2015=5\cdot13\cdot31$, only $s=1,5,13$ remain.

Cubes modulo $9$ are $0,1,-1$. Their sum is $1$ modulo $9$, so one variable is $0$ and the other $1$ modulo $3$. Thus $x+y\equiv1\pmod3$ and $s\equiv2\pmod3$, forcing $s=5$.

Now $x+y=-5$ and $x^2-xy+y^2=403$, so $xy=-126$. The roots of $t^2+5t-126$ are $9,-14$. Both ordered pairs $(9,-14),(-14,9)$ work.

statement: The board initially contains $2015$. Players alternate splitting one entry $x$ into positive integers $y,z$ with $y+z=x$. As soon as all entries are pairwise coprime, the player who just moved loses. Determine which player can force a win.
ratingReason: Duplicated multisets plus one odd entry give the strategy, but the misère ending requires checking when a mirrored split might itself lose.
solution:
The second player wins. Maintain, just before the first player moves, two identical multisets $X,X$ and one odd entry $u$; initially $X$ is empty and $u=2015$.

If the first player splits an entry $x$ of one copy of $X$, mirror that split in the other copy. If $x>2$, the two copies of the larger child are at least $2$, so the position is not pairwise coprime. If $x=2$, mirroring changes the remaining $2$ into two ones. Were that to end the game, all other entries would be ones apart from the odd singleton $u$; the first player's preceding split would already have produced a pairwise-coprime position. Thus the reply is safe whenever a reply is needed.

If the first player splits $u=y+z$ with $y>z$, split $y$ into $z$ and $y-z$. This restores the pattern with the new odd singleton $y-z$. If $z>1$, the duplicate $z$ prevents losing. If $z=1$, any existing duplicate larger than $1$ prevents losing; if none exists, the first player has already lost.

Each move increases the number of entries while preserving their sum $2015$, so play terminates. The second player always has a safe reply and therefore wins.

statement: Find all primes $p$ and nonnegative integers $m,n$ satisfying $m^3=1+p^n$.
ratingReason: The two factors of m³−1 share only a factor of three; a valuation check eliminates the apparent p=3 family.
solution:
If $n=0$ then $m^3=2$, impossible. Thus $m>1$ and
$$p^n=(m-1)(m^2+m+1).$$
If $m-1=1$, then $m=2$ and $(p,n)=(7,1)$. Otherwise both factors are divisible by $p$, which must divide $3$ after setting $m\equiv1\pmod p$. Hence $p=3$ and $m=1+3k$.

But $m^2+m+1=3(1+3k+3k^2)$ has exactly one factor of $3$, so, being a power of $3$, it must equal $3$. This is impossible for $m>1$. The only triple is $(p,m,n)=(7,2,1)$.

statement: A point starts at the origin and travels along straight segments in any of six directions spaced $60^\circ$ apart. Describe all endpoints reachable with total travel at most $10$, and find the perimeter of that region.
ratingReason: The hexagonal boundary is intuitive, but a complete proof needs both an attainable path and a lower bound ruling out every exterior point.
solution:
Let $u_1,\ldots,u_6$ be the six allowed unit direction vectors. An endpoint has the form $\sum t_i u_i$, where $t_i\ge0$ and $\sum t_i\le10$. It therefore lies in the convex hull of $10u_1,\ldots,10u_6$ (the origin also belongs to this hull).

Conversely any point in that convex hull is a convex combination $\sum\lambda_i10u_i$, with nonnegative coefficients summing to $1$. Following the corresponding six segments reaches it with total length $10$. Thus the region is a closed regular hexagon of circumradius, and side length, $10$. Its perimeter is $\boxed{60}$.

statement: For $n\ge2$, count integer tuples $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ such that $a_1=0$, every later entry differs by at most $1$ from some earlier entry, and exactly $n-1$ distinct integers occur.
ratingReason: The visited integers always form an interval. Isolating the unique repetition then makes the extensions independently countable.
solution:
There is exactly one step $m\in\{2,\ldots,n\}$ that repeats an earlier value. Before and after that step, the distinct values form an integer interval; each new value must extend one of its two ends by one.

For fixed $m$, the repeated entry has $m-1$ choices. Each of the other $n-2$ steps independently extends the upper or lower end, giving $2^{n-2}$ choices. Hence the total is
$$\sum_{m=2}^n(m-1)2^{n-2}=\boxed{2^{n-3}n(n-1)}.$$

statement: Three circles are pairwise externally tangent, and their centres lie on a circle of radius $R$. Prove that the sum of their areas is less than $4\pi R^2$.

statement: A square is divided into finitely many triangles. Prove that the sum of the diameters of the triangles’ incircles exceeds the side length of the square.

solution:
Let the square have side $s$. Euclidean edge length is at most the sum of those two displacements, with a strict inequality for at least one edge of a nondegenerate triangle.

For each triangle, area equals inradius times semiperimeter, and so is less than $2s$ times its inradius. Summing gives $s^2<s\sum d_i$, where $d_i$ are the incircle diameters. Thus $\sum d_i>s$.

statement: Determine all odd primes $p,q$ and positive integers $x,y$ satisfying $x^p+y^q=pq$.
ratingReason: An exponential size estimate first forces a unit variable; Fermat and a lift modulo q² then collapse the two primes to one.
solution:
For every integer $k\ge3$, $2^k>k^2/2$. Thus, if $x,y\ge2$,
$$x^p+y^q\ge2^p+2^q>(p^2+q^2)/2\ge pq,$$
a contradiction. Suppose $x=1$, the other case being symmetric. Then $1+y^q=pq$. Modulo $q$, Fermat gives $y\equiv-1\pmod q$. Writing $y=-1+kq$ and expanding modulo $q^2$ gives $1+y^q\equiv0\pmod{q^2}$, so $p=q$.

Now $q^2=1+y^q$. Necessarily $y\ge2$. For integers $q\ge5$, $2^q>q^2$ (induction from $q=5$), impossible. Hence $q=3$ and $y=2$. The complete answer is $(p,q,x,y)=(3,3,1,2),(3,3,2,1)$.

statement: Three cities $A,B,C$ are joined by some nonnegative numbers of direct links. A route uses either one link or two links through the third city. There are $43$ routes from $A$ to $B$ and $29$ from $B$ to $C$. What are the possible numbers of routes from $A$ to $C$?
ratingReason: Translating the route counts gives a coupled Diophantine system; adding and subtracting produces restrictive divisor conditions.
solution:
Let $x,y,z$ count the direct links $AB,BC,AC$. Then $x+yz=43$ and $y+xz=29$, so
$$(x+y)(z+1)=72,\qquad(y-x)(z-1)=14.$$
If $z=0$, then $(x,y)=(43,29)$ and $z+xy=1247$. The value $z=1$ is impossible. For $z\ge2$, the positive divisor $z-1$ of $14$ leaves $z=2,3,8,15$; the first equation eliminates $15$, and $3$ gives nonintegral $x,y$. The remaining solutions are $(x,y,z)=(5,19,2),(3,5,8)$, giving $97$ and $23$ routes. All three configurations are valid, so the answer is $\boxed{23,97,1247}$.

statement: A token starts in the centre cell of an $11\times11$ board. solution:
Yes. During the first four turns, place one wall on an outside edge at each of the four corner cells. The token needs at least six moves to leave the board from the centre, so these moves are safe.

Every boundary cell now has at most one unblocked edge leading outside. After each later move, if the token is in a boundary cell, block that edge if it is still open. Otherwise place any available wall. The token therefore never starts a move next to an unblocked outside edge. It cannot escape; eventually all outside edges can be blocked.

statement:
How many functions $f:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ satisfy $f(0)=2011$, $f(1)=111$, and
$$f(\max\{x+y+2,xy\})=\min\{f(x+y),f(xy+2)\}$$
for all nonnegative integers $x,y$?
ratingReason: Two small substitutions force the entire infinite tail to be constant; checking the exceptional initial arguments is essential to count all functions.
solution:
Putting $y=0$ gives $f(n+2)=\min\{f(n),f(2)\}$, so $f(2),f(3),f(4),\ldots$ alternates between $c=f(2)$ and $\min(111,c)$. Putting $x=y=1$ gives $f(4)=\min(f(2),f(3))$, forcing $c\le111$. Thus the whole tail from $2$ onwards is $c$.

Conversely, every integer $c\in[0,111]$ works. The left-hand argument is always at least $2$, hence its value is $c$. The argument $xy+2$ also gives $c$, while $f(x+y)$ is either $2011$, $111$ or $c$, all at least $c$. Therefore the answer is $\boxed{112}$.

statement: Take four distinct lines of the form $y=kx-k^2$, where their parameters $k$ are distinct integers. Choose four distinct intersection points so that each of the four lines contains exactly two chosen points. Write their coordinates as $(x_i,y_i)$ with $x_1\le x_2\le x_3\le x_4$. Prove $x_1+x_4=x_2+x_3$ and $y_1y_4=y_2y_3$.
ratingReason: The incidence condition is a four-cycle; identifying the smallest and largest intersection sums as opposite edges then proves both identities at once.
solution:
Lines with parameters $a,b$ intersect at $(a+b,ab)$; no three of these lines are concurrent. Regard each chosen point as an edge joining its two line parameters. Every vertex has degree two, so the four chosen edges form a four-cycle.

Call the edge with smallest sum $ab$, its opposite edge $cd$, and its neighbours $ac,bd$. From $a+b\le a+c$ and $a+b\le b+d$ we get $b\le c$ and $a\le d$. Consequently $c+d\ge a+c,b+d$, so $cd$ has largest sum. Opposite edge pairs use every parameter exactly once. Their coordinate sums are both $a+b+c+d$, and their products of second coordinates are both $abcd$. These are the required identities.

statement: Let $a_1=2010$. For $n\ge2$, let $a_n$ be the least integer greater than $a_{n-1}$ that is divisible by $n$. Prove that $a_{100},a_{101},a_{102},\ldots$ form an arithmetic progression.
ratingReason: A crude cumulative bound is enough to enter a stable range; the main insight is to express a_n as n times a fixed multiplier.
solution:
Each increment is at most $n$, so
$$a_{100}\le2010+\sum_{n=2}^{100}n=7059<10000.$$
Write $a_{100}=100k$, where $1\le k<100$. If $a_n=nk$ for $n\ge100$, then
$$(n+1)(k-1)<nk<(n+1)k.$$
Thus the least multiple of $n+1$ greater than $a_n$ is $(n+1)k$. Induction gives $a_n=nk$ for every $n\ge100$, an arithmetic progression with common difference $k$.

statement: The side lengths $a,b,c$ of a triangle satisfy $(a+b+c)(a+b-c)=2b^2$. Find the greatest possible angle opposite $a$, and determine the triangle’s angles when that maximum is attained.

statement: Finitely many cells of an infinite square grid are red. Prove that they can all be covered by finitely many grid-aligned squares with pairwise disjoint interiors, so that the proportion of red cells in each square lies between $1/5$ and $4/5$, inclusive.
ratingReason: A repeated four-way subdivision controls the overshoot in density; proving termination is the crucial complement to the construction.
solution:
If there are no red cells, use no squares. Otherwise enclose them in a sufficiently large grid square of power-of-two side length whose red density is below $1/5$. Split this square into four equal squares. Discard empty children, keep children of density at least $1/5$, and subdivide the remaining children again.

A child of a subdivided square has density less than $4/5$, because its parent has density below $1/5$. Therefore every kept square has density in the required interval. The process stops: a one-cell nonempty square would have density $1$, and so cannot arise as a child of a square still requiring subdivision. Squares kept at different stages have disjoint interiors, and every red cell is eventually in a kept square.

statement: Can five square mats with side lengths $2,2,2.1,2.5,2.5$ fit inside a square room of side $6$ without overlapping? Rotation is allowed.

The diamond with vertices $(2,3),(3.5,1.5),(5,3),(3.5,4.5)$ has no interior overlap with these four squares: each neighbouring corner lies on its boundary, which is $|x-3.5|+|y-3|=1.5$. Its side is $3/\sqrt2>2.1$, so it contains the remaining mat.

statement: Find all integer solutions of $x+x^3=5y^2$.
ratingReason: Coprimality splits the factors into two square patterns; one is excluded between consecutive squares and the other by fourth-power residues.
solution:
Since $x(1+x^2)=5y^2$, we have $x\ge0$. If $x=0$, then $y=0$. For $x>0$, the factors $x$ and $x^2+1$ are coprime. Hence either $x=5s^2$ and $x^2+1=t^2$, or $x=s^2$ and $x^2+1=5t^2$, for positive integers $s,t$.

The first is impossible because $x^2<x^2+1<(x+1)^2$. The second gives $s^4+1\equiv0\pmod5$, whereas a fourth power modulo $5$ is $0$ or $1$. Thus the only solution is $\boxed{(0,0)}$.

statement: A semicircle of radius $1$ has diameter $AB$ and centre $O$. A point $P$ lies inside it on the radius perpendicular to $AB$, with $OP=d$. The ray $AP$ meets the semicircle again at $C$, and the line through $P$ perpendicular to $PC$ meets the semicircle at $D$. Through $C$ draw a parallel to $PD$, and through $D$ a parallel to $PC$; they meet at $E$. Find $OE$ in terms of $d$.
ratingReason: Recognizing the rectangle gives a short squared-distance identity, avoiding a lengthy coordinate computation.
solution:
The quadrilateral $PCED$ is a rectangle. For any point $O$, the sums of squared distances to opposite vertices of a rectangle are equal:
$$OP^2+OE^2=OC^2+OD^2.$$
This follows directly by expanding the four squared vector lengths. Here $OC=OD=1$ and $OP=d$, so $\boxed{OE=\sqrt{2-d^2}}$.

statement: Each cell of a $17\times17$ board contains a coin, initially heads up. A move flips five consecutive coins in a horizontal, vertical or either diagonal direction. Can every coin be made tails up?
ratingReason: A five-colouring that intersects every permitted segment once turns the goal into incompatible parity requirements.
solution:
No. Number rows and columns from $0$ to $16$, and colour cell $(i,j)$ by $i+2j\pmod5$. Along any allowed direction the colour changes by a nonzero residue modulo $5$, so every move flips exactly one coin of each colour.

Four colour classes contain $58$ cells and the other contains $57$ (counting the residue classes of the row and column indices gives these sizes). If every coin ended tails up, the total number of flips in each colour class would have the parity of its size. But it is the same number—the number of moves—for every colour. The differing parities make this impossible.

statement: A convex polygon has interior angles that are positive integer multiples of $36^\circ$. (a) What is the largest possible number of sides? (b) Prove that if it has more than five sides, some two sides are parallel.
ratingReason: Exterior-angle quantization bounds the number of sides and restricts all unoriented side directions to five classes.
solution:
Every exterior angle is a positive multiple of $36^\circ$ and their sum is $360^\circ$. Thus there are at most ten sides; a regular decagon attains ten.

As we traverse the boundary, every side direction differs from the first by an integer multiple of $36^\circ$. Modulo $180^\circ$ there are only five such directions. With more than five sides, the pigeonhole principle gives two in the same class, hence parallel.

statement: There are $n$ people holding respectively $1,2,\ldots,n$ flowers. The person initially holding one flower meets every other person once, in an order of their choice. At each meeting they receive one flower if the other person currently holds more. What is the smallest possible final number of flowers they can hold?
ratingReason: A lower bound comes from counting everyone initially above the eventual total; reverse order attains it.
solution:
Let the final total be $N$. Each of the $n-N$ people who initially held more than $N$ must have given a flower, so $N-1\ge n-N$. Thus $N\ge\lceil(n+1)/2\rceil=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$.

Meet the other people in descending order $n,n-1,\ldots,2$. At the $k$th meeting, if a flower has been received at every earlier meeting, the traveller holds $k$ and the other person holds $n-k+1$. A flower is received exactly while $2k<n+1$, giving $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ gifts. All later holdings are too small to give one. This attains the bound.

statement: For each $n=2,3,\ldots,2007$, two players alternately place a domino on two empty adjacent cells of a $1\times n$ strip. A player unable to move loses. Prove that the first player has a winning strategy for at least $1505$ of these values of $n$.

statement: A collection of white, black and red pearls has total value $2107$. Their individual values are respectively $5,7,12$. The pearls are divided among at least two sisters so that each receives the same number and the same value, with differing colour compositions. The value received by each sister equals the total number of pearls in the whole collection. What colour counts can a sister choose if she maximizes the possible number of red pearls in her share?
ratingReason: A square-divisor constraint fixes the number of sisters, after which a small linear Diophantine equation determines the extreme colour composition.
solution:
Let there be $f$ sisters, each receiving $n$ pearls. Each receives value $fn$, so $f^2n=2107=7^2\cdot43$. As $f\ge2$, we get $f=7,n=43$ and value $301$ per sister.

For any sister, write her counts as $w,b,r$. Then $w+b+r=43$ and $5w+7b+12r=301$, giving $2b+7r=86$. Thus $r$ is even and at most $12$. The seven possible values $r=0,2,4,6,8,10,12$ give seven valid, distinct compositions. These compositions show that the maximum can be attained consistently with the other shares. For the largest $r=12$, the equations give $b=1,w=30$.

statement: Find all positive integer triples $(a,b,c)$ satisfying $a^{b^c}=(b^a)^c$.
ratingReason: Substituting d=b^c reduces the problem to the integer equation x^y=y^x; a coprime-factor argument classifies its exceptional unequal solutions.
solution:
Put $d=b^c$. The equation becomes $a^d=d^a$. Equal values give the entire family $a=b^c$.

For unequal positive integers $x<y$ satisfying $x^y=y^x$, neither is $1$. Write $x=gu,y=gv$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$. Taking the $g$th root gives $g^{v-u}u^v=v^u$. Any prime dividing $u$ would divide the left side but not the right, so $u=1$. Hence $g^{v-1}=v$. Since $g\ge2$ and $2^{v-1}>v$ for $v\ge3$, necessarily $v=g=2$. Thus the only unequal pair is $\{x,y\}=\{2,4\}$.

Consequently the additional triples are $\boxed{(2,4,1),(2,2,2),(4,2,1)}$, together with all $\boxed{a=b^c}$ for positive integers $b,c$.

statement: Find all integers $a,b$ for which $a^6+1\mid b^{11}-2023b^3+40b$ and $a^4-1\mid b^{10}-2023b^2-41$. Here $u\mid v$ means $v=uc$ for some integer $c$, including when $u=0$.

solution:
Every pair $(0,b)$ works. Conversely, put $d=a^2+1$, which divides both divisors and hence both right-hand expressions. Subtracting $b$ times the second expression from the first gives $d\mid81b$.

Since $a^2+1$ is never divisible by $3$, we have $\gcd(d,81)=1$, so $d\mid b$. The second expression now gives $d\mid41$. Thus $d=1$ or $41$. The latter would require $a^2=40$, impossible. Hence $a=0$, with arbitrary integer $b$.

statement:
For the side lengths $a,b,c$ of a triangle, prove
$$\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{ab}+\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{bc}+\frac{c^2+a^2-b^2}{ca}>2.$$
Show that no larger constant can replace $2$.
ratingReason: The cosine rule transforms the expression into a familiar but strict angle inequality; a limiting family is needed to establish sharpness.
solution:
Let the opposite angles be $A,B,C$. The left side is $2(\cos A+\cos B+\cos C)$. Since $|A-B|<A+B<\pi$,
$$\cos A+\cos B=2\cos\frac{A+B}{2}\cos\frac{A-B}{2}>2\cos^2\frac{A+B}{2}=1-\cos C.$$
This proves the strict bound. To show it is best possible, take $A=2t$, $B=C=\pi/2-t$ and let $t$ decrease to zero. The left side is $2\cos(2t)+4\sin t$, which tends to $2$.

statement: Find all functions $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfying $f(f(x)+y)=f(y)+x$ for all positive $x,y$.
ratingReason: Evaluating a nested expression in two ways yields additivity; positivity gives monotonicity, which rigidifies the resulting involution.
solution:
Evaluate $f(f(f(x)+y)+z)$ in two ways. Direct use of the equation gives $f(z)+f(x)+y$. Replacing the inner value by $f(y)+x$ first gives $f(x+z)+y$. Hence $f(x+z)=f(x)+f(z)$ for all positive $x,z$.

Positivity makes $f$ strictly increasing. Additivity in the original equation also gives $f(f(x))=x$. If $f(x)>x$, increasingness gives $x=f(f(x))>f(x)$, a contradiction; the reverse inequality is equally impossible. Thus $\boxed{f(x)=x}$, which works.

statement: Find all primes $p$ and positive integers $n$ such that $n5^{n-n/p}=p!(p^2+1)+n$.
ratingReason: Prime valuations first force p to divide n; Fermat and Wilson then identify the prime, leaving a monotone exponential equation.
solution:
The equation makes $5^{n/p}$ rational. If it is $u/v$ in lowest terms, then $u^p=5^n v^p$; comparing prime exponents forces $v=1$ and $p\mid n$. Write $n=kp$ and divide by $p$:
$$k5^{k(p-1)}=(p-1)!(p^2+1)+k.$$
If $p\ne5$, Fermat and Wilson reduce this modulo $p$ to $k\equiv-1+k$, impossible. Thus $p=5$ and
$$k(5^{4k}-1)=24\cdot26=624.$$
The left side strictly increases for positive integer $k$, and equals $624$ at $k=1$. Therefore $\boxed{p=n=5}$.

statement: Triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ have $EF\parallel BC$, $FD\parallel CA$, and $DE\parallel AB$. Reflect the lines $EF,FD,DE$ in $BC,CA,AB$, respectively. If the three reflected lines are concurrent, determine the ratio $[DEF]:[ABC]$.

solution:
Let $P$ be the common point of the reflected lines. Let $D'=2A-P$, using vector notation. For a line parallel to $AB$, reflection in $AB$ sends its points to points whose signed perpendicular distance from $AB$ is negated. Since $P$ is on the reflected image of $DE$, and $A$ is on $AB$, the point $D'$ lies on $DE$. The same argument with $AC$ shows $D'$ lies on $DF$. Hence $D=D'=2A-P$.

Similarly, $E=2B-P$ and $F=2C-P$. Thus $DEF$ is the image of $ABC$ under the homothety with centre $P$ and factor $2$. The area ratio is $\boxed{4:1}$.

statement: Ten boxes each hold at most $2021$ index cards. For each chicken, copies of its card may be placed in several boxes. Any seven boxes together must contain a card for every chicken. What is the largest possible number of chickens?
ratingReason: Four-copy redundancy gives a capacity bound, and a balanced cyclic construction must attain the integer bound despite the leftover spaces.

Each chicken needs cards in at least four different boxes, or losing three boxes could lose all its cards. Thus the number of chickens is at most $\lfloor20210/4\rfloor=5052$.

For a block of ten chickens, put their cards in the ten cyclic blocks of four consecutive boxes. This uses four slots in every box. Repeat for $505$ blocks, covering $5050$ chickens and using $2020$ slots in each box. Use eight of the ten remaining slots for four copies each of two more chickens. Every chicken is represented in four boxes, so any seven boxes contain it. The maximum is $\boxed{5052}$.

statement: At $n\ge2$ distinguished seats around a circular table, place napkins of three available colours, one per seat, with neighbouring seats always different. How many arrangements are possible? Rotations of the seat assignment are counted separately.
ratingReason: Conditioning on whether two vertices at distance two share a colour yields a recurrence; solving it gives the cycle-colouring formula.
solution:
Let $a_n$ be the answer. We have $a_2=a_3=6$. For $n\ge4$, consider three consecutive vertices $A,B,C$. If $A,C$ have different colours, contracting the path through $B$ gives a proper colouring of a cycle of length $n-1$, and $B$ has one forced colour. If $A,C$ have the same colour, identify them, obtaining a cycle of length $n-2$; $B$ has two choices. Thus $a_n=a_{n-1}+2a_{n-2}$.

The expression $2^n+2(-1)^n$ satisfies this recurrence and both initial values. Therefore the answer is $\boxed{2^n+2(-1)^n}$.

statement: Find all positive integers $k$ for which some positive integers $a_1,\ldots,a_{k+1}$ satisfy $a_1!+\cdots+a_{k+1}!=k!$.
ratingReason: Bounding how many summands can attain the largest available factorial leaves a gap between possible totals; the small cases must be separated.
solution:
Every $a_i<k$, since all summands are positive. Suppose $k>3$ and exactly $m$ of the $a_i$ equal $k-1$. We must have $m\le k-1$, as $k$ such summands already total $k!$. Hence
$$\sum a_i!\le[m(k-1)+(k+1-m)](k-2)!\le[k(k-1)-(k-3)](k-2)!<k!,$$
a contradiction. For $k=1,2$ the sum of $k+1$ positive factorials already exceeds $k!$. For $k=3$, the example $1!+1!+2!+2!=3!$ works. Thus $\boxed{k=3}$.

statement: Positive integers $a\ge b$ satisfy $\sqrt{a+\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}\in\mathbb Z$. Prove that $a$ and $b$ have the same parity.
ratingReason: Squaring twice exposes a square quotient and a parametrization by two integers of the same parity, avoiding a longer coprime-factor case split.
solution:
Let the outer square root be the positive integer $c$. Then $b^2=c^2(2a-c^2)$. The integer $2a-c^2=(b/c)^2$ is a rational square, hence an integer square: write it as $t^2$ with positive integer $t$. Thus $2a=c^2+t^2$ and $b=ct$.

Because $c^2+t^2$ is even, $c,t$ have the same parity. If both are even then $a,b$ are even. If both are odd, their squares are $1$ modulo $4$, so $a$ is odd and $b$ is odd. In either case the parities agree.

statement: Prove that $\prod_{j=0}^{1009}(x-j)^2=c$ has $2020$ distinct real solutions whenever $0<c<(1009\cdot1007\cdots3\cdot1)^4/2^{2020}$.
ratingReason: The degree gives the upper bound, but the lower bound needs a uniform estimate at every half-integer between consecutive zeros and continuity in all intervals.
solution:
Let $P(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{1009}(x-j)^2$. At consecutive half-integers $t,t+1$ between its integer zeros,
$$\frac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}=\left(\frac{t+1}{1009-t}\right)^2.$$
Thus these values decrease towards the central point $1009/2$ and then increase. Their minimum is
$$P(1009/2)=\frac{(1\cdot3\cdots1009)^4}{2^{2020}}>c.$$
In each of the $1009$ intervals between consecutive integer zeros, continuity gives one solution on each side of its midpoint. There is also a solution to the left of $0$ and to the right of $1009$, since $P$ tends to infinity in both directions. These give $2020$ distinct solutions. The polynomial $P-c$ has degree $2020$, so there are no more.

In triangle $CBF$, the line $FO$ is a median. It meets $CE$ at the point dividing $CE$ in ratio $2:1$ from $C$. This forces $Q$ to be the centroid and $E$ to be the midpoint of $BF$ (equivalently, apply the converse of the centroid ratio). statement: Find all positive integer pairs $(m,n)$ satisfying $mn-1\mid n^3-1$, using the convention that $u\mid v$ means $v=ku$ for an integer $k$.
ratingReason: Repeated reduction makes the asymmetric condition symmetric; comparing each positive remainder with the divisor forces one of two square relations.
solution:
All pairs with $m=1$ or $n=1$ work, as do those with $m=n^2$ or $n=m^2$. Suppose now $m,n>1$ and put $d=mn-1$. Reduction modulo $d$ successively gives
$$d\mid n^2-m,\qquad d\mid n-m^2,\qquad d\mid m^3-1.$$
Since $d\mid n^3-1$ and $d\mid m^3-1$, we obtain $m\le n^2$ and $n\le m^2$. If both inequalities are strict, the positive divisible integers satisfy $d\le n^2-m$ and $d\le m^2-n$. The former implies $m<n$, and the latter $n<m$, impossible. Thus one equality holds, completing the classification.

statement: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(2019)=1$ and $f(x)f(y)+f(2019/x)f(2019/y)=2f(xy)$ for all nonzero $x,y$.
ratingReason: Simple substitutions yield inversion symmetry and multiplicativity; using positive numbers as squares eliminates pathological multiplicative possibilities.
solution:
Set $(x,y)=(1,2019)$ to obtain $f(1)=1$. Then $y=1$ gives $f(2019/x)=f(x)$, so the equation simplifies to $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$. Consequently $f(x)^2=f(x)f(2019/x)=f(2019)=1$.

For $x>0$, write $x=t^2$ to get $f(x)=f(t)^2=1$. For $x<0$, multiplicativity gives $f(x)=f(-1)f(-x)=f(-1)$, where $f(-1)=\pm1$. Thus the solutions are the constant function $1$ and the sign function. Both satisfy the equation.

statement: For odd positive $n$, let $n!!=n(n-2)\cdots3\cdot1$. How many different residues modulo $1000$ occur among $1!!,3!!,5!!,\ldots$?
ratingReason: Separating the modulus into eight and125 turns the infinite tail into a short cycle, while the initial values need a careful finite count.
solution:
For $n\ge25$, $125\mid n!!$. Modulo $8$, successive odd factors repeat $1,3,5,7$, whose product is $1$. Thus the double factorial residues cycle as $1,3,7,1$ modulo $8$. By the Chinese remainder theorem, the tail has exactly three residues modulo $1000$: $625,875,375$.

For $n=1,3,\ldots,23$, successive multiplication modulo $1000$ gives
$$1,3,15,105,945,395,135,25,425,75,575,225.$$
These twelve residues are distinct and none is divisible by $125$. Hence there are $\boxed{15}$ residues altogether.

statement: Find all real polynomials $P$ satisfying $P(x)+3P(x+2)=3P(x+1)+P(x+3)$ for every real $x$.
ratingReason: Recognizing a third finite difference turns the translation identity into a degree constraint.
solution: Define $\Delta P(x)=P(x+1)-P(x)$. The equation is exactly $\Delta^3P=0$. A nonconstant polynomial of degree $d$ has finite difference of degree $d-1$, since its leading term $ax^d$ contributes $ad x^{d-1}$. Therefore the third difference vanishes precisely for polynomials of degree at most two, including the zero polynomial. The answer is $\boxed{P(x)=ax^2+bx+c}$ with arbitrary real $a,b,c$.

statement: Find all real polynomials $P$ satisfying $\sum_{j=0}^{2018}(-1)^j\binom{2018}{j}P(x+j)=0$ for every real $x$.

solution:
For $\Delta f(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)$, induction using Pascal’s identity gives
$$\Delta^r f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^{r-j}\binom rj f(x+j).$$
Since $2018$ is even, the equation says $\Delta^{2018}P=0$. Each finite difference lowers the degree of a nonconstant polynomial by exactly one and sends a constant to zero. Thus the solutions are exactly all real polynomials of degree at most $2017$, including zero.

statement: An integer sequence is valid if every even entry is followed by half that entry, and every odd entry is followed by an integer differing from it by $1$. Find the shortest possible length of a valid sequence starting at $2018$ and ending at $1$.
ratingReason: A short path is easy to find, but proving minimality requires controlling both choices at every odd value; a decreasing recurrence makes the optimization rigorous.
solution:
Let $L(n)$ be the minimum number of entries, including both ends, for a sequence from $n$ to1. Then $L(1)=1$; for even $n$, $L(n)=1+L(n/2)$; and for odd $n\ge3$,
$$L(n)=2+\min\{L((n-1)/2),L((n+1)/2)\}.$$
The last recurrence includes the forced division after either odd-number move, so all arguments on its right are smaller. It proves minimality as well as providing a computation. In particular $L(2^j)=j+1$, and successive use gives
$$\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}n&3&7&15&31&63&127&253&505&1009\\\hline L(n)&3&5&6&7&8&9&11&12&13\end{array}$$
(the intermediate even values use the first recurrence). Hence $L(2018)=14$. A sequence attaining it is
$$2018,1009,1008,504,252,126,63,64,32,16,8,4,2,1.$$

statement: Let $a_0=2$, $a_1=15$, and $a_{n+2}=15a_{n+1}+16a_n$ for $n\ge0$. Prove that $269$ divides infinitely many terms of the sequence.
ratingReason: Solving the recurrence exposes a power of two whose exponent aligns with Fermat’s theorem and the alternating sign.
solution:
Induction on the recurrence gives $a_n=16^n+(-1)^n$. The number $269$ is prime: none of $2,3,5,7,11,13$ divides it. Fermat therefore gives $2^{268}\equiv1\pmod{269}$.

For any nonnegative integer $t$, take $n=67(2t+1)$. Then $n$ is odd and $4n=268(2t+1)$, so $a_n=2^{4n}-1\equiv0\pmod{269}$. These are infinitely many distinct indices.

statement: Fix $a>0$ and $0<\alpha<\pi$. Triangle $ABC$ has $BC=a$, $\angle BAC=\alpha$, circumcentre $O$ and orthocentre $H$. A point $P$ lies on the ray from $A$ through $O$. Reflect $P$ in $AC$ and $AB$ to obtain $S,T$. If $S,A,T,H$ are concyclic, prove that $AP$ depends only on $a$ and $\alpha$.
ratingReason: The isogonal relationship between the circumcentre and orthocentre makes AH a diameter of an auxiliary circle; the sine rule then removes the remaining triangle shape.
solution:
Use vectors with $A$ as origin, and write $P=tO$ with $t>0$. Put $R=AO$. Since $O$ is equidistant from $A,B,C$, its reflection in $AB$ is $B-O$, and its reflection in $AC$ is $C-O$. Also the orthocentre vector is $H=B+C-2O$. Consequently $S+T=tH$ and $|S|=|T|=tR$.

Let $K$ be the centre of the circle through $A,S,T,H$. As $A=0$, the circle equation is $|X|^2=2K\cdot X$. Applying it at $S,T$ and adding gives $2t^2R^2=2tK\cdot H=t|H|^2$. Hence $t=|H|^2/(2R^2)$. The standard identity $AH=2R|\cos\alpha|$ and the sine rule $a=2R\sin\alpha$ now yield
$$AP=tR=2R\cos^2\alpha=\boxed{\frac{a\cos^2\alpha}{\sin\alpha}}.$$
The cyclic configuration is nondegenerate, so the right-angle case with $H=A$ does not arise.

statement: A walking sequence satisfies $a_{i+1}=a_i\pm1$. Prove that there is an integer sequence $b_1,\ldots,b_{2016}$ such that every walking sequence $a_1,\ldots,a_{2016}$ with $1\le a_i\le1010$ has $a_j=b_j$ for some $j$.
ratingReason: A single sweep cannot catch both parity classes. Two opposite sweeps with a repeated peak handle them separately by a discrete crossing argument.
solution:
Choose $b_i=i+1$ for $1\le i\le1008$, and $b_i=2018-i$ for $1009\le i\le2016$. Thus the sequence rises from $2$ to $1009$, repeats $1009$, and descends to $2$.

For a walking sequence, the parity of $i+a_i$ is constant. If it is odd, compare the first sweep. At $i=1$, $a_1$ is even, so $a_1\ge b_1$; at $i=1008$, $a_i$ is odd, so $a_i\le1009=b_i$. The even differences $a_i-b_i$ change only by $0$ or $-2$, so one is zero.

If the parity is even, compare the second sweep. At $i=1009$, $a_i$ is odd and at most $1009=b_i$; at $i=2016$, $a_i$ is even and at least $2=b_i$. Here the even differences change only by $0$ or $2$, so again one is zero.

statement: Find all nonnegative integers $x,y,z$ satisfying $x^3+2y^3+4z^3=9!$.
ratingReason: Repeated divisibility by two cycles the weighted cubic form; cubic residues modulo nine then reduce the large equation to a tiny bounded search.
solution:
Modulo $9$, cubes are $0,\pm1$. The only way a sum $u+2v+4w$ with $u,v,w\in\{0,\pm1\}$ is zero modulo $9$ is $u=v=w=0$. Therefore $3$ divides $x,y,z$. Writing $x=3X,y=3Y,z=3Z$ gives $X^3+2Y^3+4Z^3=13440=2^7\cdot105$.

An even right side forces the variable with coefficient one to be even. Substitute twice that variable and divide by two; the coefficients cycle from $(1,2,4)$ to $(4,1,2)$. Repeating seven times gives $X=8c,Y=4a,Z=4b$ and
$$a^3+2b^3+4c^3=105.$$
Here $a$ is odd, so $a=1$ or $3$, while $b\le3,c\le2$. If $a=1$, the sum is at most $1+54+32=87$. If $c\le1$, it is at most $27+54+4=85$. Thus $a=3,c=2$, leaving $2b^3=46$, impossible. There are no solutions, including cases with a zero variable.

statement:
Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that, for all distinct real $x,y$,
$$f(x)f(y)=|x-y|\,f\!\left(\frac{xy+1}{x-y}\right).$$
ratingReason: A carefully chosen fixed output collapses the equation once nonvanishing is established; the fractional argument and absolute value complicate routine substitutions.
solution:
The zero function works. Suppose $f(z)\ne0$ for some $z$. For every $y\ne z$, solve $xy+zy-xz+1=0$ for $x$. This relation is equivalent to $(xy+1)/(x-y)=z$; it cannot have $x=y$ over the reals. The equation then forces $f(y)\ne0$, so $f$ never vanishes.

For any $y$, choose $x=y+\sqrt{y^2+1}$. Then $x\ne y$ and $(xy+1)/(x-y)=x$. Cancelling $f(x)$ gives $f(y)=|x-y|=\sqrt{y^2+1}$. Finally,
$$(x-y)^2+(xy+1)^2=(x^2+1)(y^2+1)$$
verifies this function. Thus the solutions are $\boxed{f\equiv0}$ and $\boxed{f(x)=\sqrt{x^2+1}}$.

statement: Positive integers $a,b,c$ count knights wearing three respective colours. Prove that they can be seated around a circular table with no same-coloured neighbours if and only if a triangle exists with side lengths $a+\tfrac12,b+\tfrac12,c+\tfrac12$.
ratingReason: The triangle condition disguises a discrete largest-colour bound; a complete seating construction proves sufficiency.
solution:
Assume $a\ge b\ge c$. Any valid seating requires at least one other-coloured knight in each gap between the $a$ knights of the first colour, so $a\le b+c$.

Conversely, seat those $a$ knights around the table. Put the $b$ knights of the second colour in distinct gaps, then fill the other $a-b$ gaps with knights of the third colour. The remaining $b+c-a\le b$ third-coloured knights can each be placed next to a different second-coloured knight in its gap. No equal colours become adjacent.

The only nontrivial triangle inequality for the three proposed side lengths is $a+1/2<b+c+1$, equivalent, for integer $a,b,c$, to $a\le b+c$.

statement: A bag contains $n$ red marbles and one black marble. A player starts with fortune $1$. Before each draw, they stake a real amount between zero and their current fortune; a red draw adds that stake, and a black draw subtracts it. Drawn marbles are removed, and play stops after $n$ draws. What is the greatest final fortune the player can guarantee, regardless of draw order?
ratingReason: Balancing the two possible first-draw outcomes yields a nonlinear recurrence; its reciprocal form telescopes and the resulting stake must be feasible.
solution:
Let $F_n$ be the optimal guarantee, with $F_0=1$. If the first stake is $x\in[0,1]$, a black draw permits doubling on the remaining $n-1$ certain red draws, giving $(1-x)2^{n-1}$. A red draw leaves a scaled version of the smaller problem, giving $(1+x)F_{n-1}$. The guaranteed amount is the minimum of these two quantities.

Their minimum is maximized where they agree, provided the intersection is in $[0,1]$. This gives
$$F_n=\frac{2^nF_{n-1}}{2^{n-1}+F_{n-1}},\qquad\frac{2^n}{F_n}=1+\frac{2^{n-1}}{F_{n-1}}.$$
Induction yields $\boxed{F_n=2^n/(n+1)}$. The required fraction staked is $(n-1)/(n+1)$, which is feasible. The two-outcome bound proves optimality as well as supplying the strategy.

statement: Find all nonnegative integers $x,y$ such that $3^x+7^y$ is a perfect square and $y$ is even.
ratingReason: Factoring a difference of squares forces one factor to be one, then the order of three modulo seven contradicts the required parity.
solution:
Squares modulo $4$ show that $x,y$ have opposite parity. Put $y=2k$ and $3^x+7^{2k}=n^2$. Then $(n-7^k)(n+7^k)=3^x$. Both factors are powers of $3$, but their difference $2\cdot7^k$ is not divisible by $3$, so the smaller factor is $1$. Hence $3^x=2\cdot7^k+1$.

If $k=0$, we get $(x,y)=(1,0)$. If $k>0$, then $3^x\equiv1\pmod7$, forcing $6\mid x$, whereas $x$ must be odd. Thus $\boxed{(1,0)}$ is the only solution.

statement: Find all nonnegative integers $x,y$ such that $3^x+7^y$ is a perfect square and $y$ is odd.
ratingReason: A difference-of-squares factorization is followed by an exponent-divisibility argument that introduces an unavoidable prime factor19.
solution:
Modulo $4$, $x$ must be even. Put $x=2k$. Factoring $n^2-3^{2k}=7^y$ shows that the two factors are powers of $7$ whose difference is $2\cdot3^k$, so the smaller is $1$. Thus $7^y=2\cdot3^k+1$.

The case $k=0$ gives no solution, while $k=1$ gives $(x,y)=(2,1)$. For $k\ge2$, divide $7^y-1=2\cdot3^k$ by $6$ to get $1+7+\cdots+7^{y-1}=3^{k-1}$. Modulo $3$ this forces $3\mid y$. But then $7^2+7+1=57=3\cdot19$ divides that geometric sum, contradicting its being a power of $3$. Therefore $\boxed{(2,1)}$ is the only solution.

statement: Nine points lie on a circle. Prove that the $36$ chords joining pairs of them can be coloured with four colours so that every set of four points has all four colours among its six joining chords.
ratingReason: The successful construction labels vertices by a two-dimensional vector space over three residues; four parallel classes and pigeonhole give the required property.
solution:
Label the nine points by the pairs $(x,y)\in\{0,1,2\}^2$. Colour a chord by which of the following expressions agrees at its endpoints, modulo $3$:
$$x,\qquad y,\qquad x+y,\qquad x-y.$$
Exactly one agrees. Indeed, two agreements would force both coordinates equal; if neither coordinate agrees, the two nonzero coordinate differences are either equal or opposite, so one of the last two expressions agrees.

For any four chosen vertices, each of these four expressions takes only three possible values. Pigeonhole supplies a pair agreeing in that expression, whose chord has the corresponding colour. Thus every colour occurs.

statement: Find all positive integer triples $(a,b,c)$ such that $(32a+3b+48c)/(4abc)$ is an integer.
ratingReason: Divisibility first forces a hidden factor16 in b; the reduced inequality then shows two variables must be one and leaves a controlled finite check.
solution:
The divisibility first implies $4\mid b$, and then $16\mid b$. Write $b=16t$; the condition becomes $4atc\mid2a+3t+3c$, so
$$4\le\frac2{tc}+\frac3{ac}+\frac3{at}.$$
The right side decreases as any variable increases. At $(a,t,c)=(1,2,2),(2,1,2),(2,2,1)$ it is respectively $3.5,3.25,3.25$, all below four. Therefore at least two variables are one.

If $t=c=1$, then $4a\mid2a+6$, yielding $a=1$ or $3$. If $a=c=1$, then $4t\mid3t+5$, yielding $t=1$ or $5$; the case $a=t=1$ similarly gives $c=1$ or $5$. Substitution confirms
$$\boxed{(a,b,c)=(1,16,1),(3,16,1),(1,80,1),(1,16,5)}.$$

statement: Let $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}=1+(a_1+\cdots+a_n)/n$. Prove that for every $\beta>0$ there is a positive integer $k$ with $a_k<\beta k$.
ratingReason: Subtracting consecutive defining equations reveals harmonic growth; a quantitative sublinear bound completes the argument without assuming logarithms.
solution:
Subtracting the equations for consecutive partial sums gives $a_{n+1}=a_n+1/n$. Thus $a_n=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}1/j$.

For $n\ge2$, Cauchy–Schwarz and $1/j^2\le1/(j(j-1))$ for $j\ge2$ give
$$a_n^2\le n\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac1{j^2}\right)<3n.$$
Choose an integer $k\ge2$ with $k>3/\beta^2$. Then $a_k<\sqrt{3k}<\beta k$, as desired.

statement: An acute triangle has longest side $s$. Prove that every point inside the triangle is at distance at most $s/\sqrt3$ from at least one vertex.
ratingReason: The circumcentre partitions the triangle into regions covered by a vertex-centred disk; the largest-angle bound controls the circumradius.
solution:
Let $O$ be the circumcentre and $R$ the circumradius. Since the triangle is acute, $O$ is inside it. Join $O$ to the vertices and side midpoints, forming six triangles. In each small triangle, one original vertex $V$ has distance at most $R$ to all three corners: the corners are $V$, $O$, and a midpoint at distance at most $R$. The closed disk of radius $R$ centred at $V$ is convex, so it covers that entire small triangle. Therefore every point is within $R$ of some original vertex.

The angle opposite the longest side lies between $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$. The extended sine rule gives $R=s/(2\sin A)\le s/\sqrt3$, completing the proof.
